title: Emergence of Physical Intelligence via Controllable Information Production
claim: An agent guided only by an intrinsic signal autonomously recovers from a failed state to stable, goal-like behavior.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right filmstrip of poses, rising trajectory
description: A single wide filmstrip of a brown stick-figure humanoid rendered on a white background, read left to right as a time sequence. On the far left the humanoid hangs upside down, with its legs up and its head near the bottom. In the middle the figure tumbles and crumples, with several overlapping poses in a tangled pile. Toward the right it pushes itself up from a crouch. The last seven poses show it standing upright with arms raised in a stable posture. The baseline of poses rises slightly from left to right, which suggests recovery. There are no labels, arrows, axes or text. The eye goes first to the tangled cluster in the middle, then follows the rising trajectory to the upright figures on the right.
caption: A humanoid-like agent discovers self-righting and stable upright behavior using Controllable Information Production (CIP) as its sole intrinsic motivation signal.
abstract: Intrinsic Motivation (IM) aims to train agents without external rewards, enabling useful behavior to emerge from the agent's interaction with its environment alone. However, the dominant IM approaches rely on information-theoretic quantities with designer-chosen variables, introducing bias and lacking a principled connection to dynamics or optimal control (OC). We introduce Controllable Information Production (CIP), a novel IM method explicitly grounded in dynamical systems and OC. CIP measures the rate at which an agent produces information, capturing controllable complexity without external knowledge or bias. CIP unifies IM and OC into a single framework, formalizing physical intelligence as the control of information production. It further reveals connections between the structure of the value function and Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy. CIP consistently outperforms prior IM methods on standard benchmarks in robot learning and solves tasks they fail on, including humanoid self-righting. These results support an organizing principle: that physical intelligence emerges from driving systems toward the edge of controllable chaos.
